abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,532 articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question–answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their steady-state reference efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 ∘C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

sections.body: The introduction argues that domain language models must link observations to mechanisms and design discriminating experiments. It presents **PSM-Bench**, with 800 expert-developed questions drawn from 446 studies, whose criteria accommodate alternative answers. OpenPerov Flash learns from evidence records reconstructed from 4,532 articles, and OpenPerov Pro retrieves evidence to refine selected passages. The authors report that Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems, that structured-evidence learning outperformed conventional question–answer adaptation with fewer training tokens, and that targeted revision gave larger gains than regenerating complete answers. As a test on a complex interface, OpenPerov prioritized BCPCz–TMPS–K over the Na analogue favoured by human experts, under matched fabrication conditions.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: The authors build a perovskite reasoning benchmark and OpenPerov, a model trained on expert-calibrated evidence records.

sections.body: This section reports results on PSM-Bench, where Flash scores 87.6 against 83.3 for GLM-5.2 and leads all four task families. Its advantage held in a double-blind expert assessment of 3,200 anonymized answers, where Flash ranked first in 99.84% of human-score bootstrap resamples. Pro raises Scientific Mastery to 89.1 by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. Structured-evidence adaptation scored 82.3 after initial training, against 71.5 for conventional adaptation. After shared targeted training, the structured route kept a 3.50-point advantage, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.60–4.34 for the paired difference. An example iodine-redistribution record illustrates how the reconstructed evidence keeps observations linked to their controls and proposed mechanism.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Flash scores 87.6 on PSM-Bench, first among 13 closed-book systems, and structured-evidence training beats question-answer training.

sections.body: The conclusion restates three claims. OpenPerov leads PSM-Bench across all its task families, a result corroborated by double-blind expert assessment. On questions from subsequent studies, Flash and Pro both outscored human experts in the experimental-context and limited-context settings. In the self-assembled monolayer (SAM) case study, OpenPerov proposed BCPCz–TMPS–K, which assigns substrate anchoring and perovskite passivation to distinct chemical units. Devices with this contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05%. The authors state that this supports OpenPerov translating scientific reasoning into molecular design. The conclusion itself gives no further numbers for the subsequent-study comparison.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: OpenPerov leads every PSM-Bench task family, and its selected self-assembled monolayer contact reached 27.05% efficiency.

sections.body: The adaptation uses LoRA adapters with rank r=16, alpha=32 and dropout 0.05 on Qwen3.6-27B. Domain-adaptive pretraining uses 78,299 structured records in 1,024-token blocks, followed by scientific instruction and answer-style training. Closed-book systems receive only the frozen questions, and Pro retrieves from 173,024 article-centred documents, keeping the top 40 articles and allowing at most two edits per answer on subsequent-study tasks. Confidence intervals use 10,000 bootstrap resamples. For the subsequent-study comparison, Pro's reported mean adds its matched gain over Flash to the previously established Flash mean. Devices use 16 independent units per group, and stability is tested under modified ISOS-LC-2 cycling, ISOS-D-2 dark ageing at 85 ∘C, and ISOS-L-1 continuous illumination.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Methods adapt a 27B model on 4,035 articles, score 800 questions, and test devices under three ageing protocols.

sections.body: The benchmark questions, reference answers, evaluation criteria, model responses, anonymized human assessments and numerical evaluation records are available in the OpenPerov GitHub repository. The released component scores and analysis scripts reproduce the evaluation summaries reported in the paper. The literature-derived training and retrieval corpora, source-support passages and evidence indexes are not publicly distributed, so the evidence records cannot be rebuilt from the release alone.
sections.heading: Data availability
sections.headline: PSM-Bench, evaluation records and human assessments are public, but literature-derived training and retrieval corpora are not.

sections.body: Code for model adaptation, inference, evidence retrieval, local revision and evaluation is available in the OpenPerov GitHub repository. The combined OpenPerov Flash adapter and the trained OpenPerov Pro retrieval adapters are provided in an OpenPerov collection on Hugging Face. Loading instructions and model cards accompany the adapters.
sections.heading: Code availability
sections.headline: Code for adaptation, retrieval, revision and evaluation is public, with the Flash adapter and Pro retrieval adapters on Hugging Face.

sections.body: The appendix provides supplementary methods numbered SM1 to SM14 and supplementary figures. SM1 describes corpus construction, including 25,848 figure-asset records and 3,819 table-asset records, and the literature lineage of 36,625 reference papers and 7,881 citing papers. SM2 gives the article-level training boundary, with 4,035 adaptation articles and 497 held-out articles. SM3 specifies the LoRA configuration, the DAPT objective and 19,334,490 training tokens. SM4 defines the PSM-Bench construction, with task families of n=368, n=300, n=73 and n=59 items. Supplementary Figures S18 to S24 cover retrieval performance, the balance of local revision, post-cutoff scoring, perovskite-stability trends, transfer to the Perovskite-R1 benchmark, and device performance.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists supplementary methods on corpus construction, training, benchmark protocol, and supplementary figures S18 to S24.
